findings.description: The RDS MySQL instance sets publicly_accessible = true, giving it an internet-routable endpoint. Combined with the exported endpoint output and the privileged 'admin' master user, this exposes the database tier directly to the internet.
storage_encrypted = false disables KMS encryption of the RDS storage volume and its snapshots, leaving stored application data unencrypted at the storage layer.

The master password is taken from var.password (a plain variable, not marked sensitive and not sourced from Secrets Manager) and the same value is interpolated into EC2 user data; it is persisted in cleartext in Terraform state and in the instance metadata.

The user_data script writes the RDS master username and plaintext password into /var/www/inc/dbinfo.inc. EC2 user data is readable from the instance metadata service by any local process or via SSRF, leaking the database master credentials.

No metadata_options block is set, so IMDSv1 (token-less metadata access) remains available. The instance runs a public-facing PHP application and carries a highly privileged instance profile, so an SSRF flaw yields role credentials and the user-data secrets.

No root_block_device with encrypted = true is specified, so the root volume - which holds the dbinfo.inc file containing the database master credentials - relies on account defaults and may be unencrypted at rest.

The inline policy grants s3:*, ec2:* and rds:* on Resource "*". Attached to an internet-reachable web instance, theft of the role credentials yields near-total control of S3 data, EC2 and RDS across the account, including resetting the RDS master password or exfiltrating snapshots.
Port 3306 is opened to the whole VPC CIDR rather than to the application server's security group, so any workload in any subnet of the VPC can reach the database, defeating tier segmentation.
The database security group permits all protocols and ports outbound to 0.0.0.0/0, providing an unconstrained exfiltration and callback path from a compromised database tier.

findings.issue_category: no TLS enforcement for DB connections
findings.description: The MySQL 8.0 parameter group sets only character-set parameters and omits require_secure_transport = 1, so the publicly accessible database accepts unencrypted client connections and credentials can traverse the network in cleartext.

The user_data installs httpd serving the PHP form over plain HTTP with no TLS configuration, and the instance's public DNS is published, so submitted form data and any session material travel unencrypted.
